# Copper October 2009 

- This year’s annual gathering of the metals industry in London during the second week of the month highlighted the divergence of view on the outlook for copper in the near term.  Market participants from the financial sector appeared optimistic while those from the physical side were less so.  In the case of the optimists, positive sentiment stemmed from the belief that the worst was over for consumers and that prices would continue to be buoyed by supply constraints, while the more downbeat mood from producers and fabricators reflected concerns over future physical demand going forward. 

- One of the biggest surprises of the month was the latest Chinese trade data which showed a 152% uplift in September’s refined copper imports.  A gain of this magnitude had not been expected given the reduction in SHFE:LME price arbitrage from June onwards and the recent build in SHFE exchange stocks and improved scrap availability.  The data suggests that Chinese apparent refined copper consumption had increased by 52% (+220kt) in September from a year earlier.  At the same time official data showed that Chinese semis production increased by 24.7% year on year in September, implying a significant stock build (regardless of the contribution from scrap). 

- Despite an improving global economic picture, demand for copper in some regions remains extremely weak.  This is especially true of Europe and the USA where the downturn in some markets has been much stronger than we previously anticipated.  As a consequence we have lowered our forecasts accordingly and now expect global refined copper consumption to fall by 4.5% this year to ~17.1Mt. 

- Unlike this time last year when spot terms in the concentrate market were rising sharply, trader quotes have fallen quite markedly during October to single digits in tandem with too much demand chasing too little supply.  Chinese spot buying terms have declined from $20/t & 2c/lb last month to $15/t & 1.5c/lb (M+1) currently.  Elsewhere, spot rates in India have also fallen over the past month, again from $20/t & 2c/lb to the $15/t & 1.5c/lb mark.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Mixed sen

timent emerged from LME week** This year’s annual gathering of the metals industry in London during the second week of the month highlighted the divergence of view on the outlook for copper in the near term.  Market participants from the financial sector appeared optimistic while those from the physical side were less so.  In the case of the optimists, positive sentiment stemmed from the belief that the worst was over for consumers and that prices would continue to be buoyed by supply constraints, while the more downbeat mood from producers and fabricators reflected concerns over future physical demand going forward. 

**Official prices trend upwards during October** During the month official (3m) prices trended upwards, rising from an October low of $5886/t on the 5<sup>th</sup> to the month’s high of $6696/t on the 26<sup>th</sup> for an average of $6298/t.  This represented the highest monthly average year-to-date and a gain of 103% (+$3191/t) from the December 2008 low of $3107/t.  Much of the October price rise appears to have been on the back of a weakening dollar and continued supply issues. 

**Supply issues provide price support** October saw its fair share of supply disruptions with a combination of further industrial action, mechanical failures and various reports of underperforming mine production.  After threatening strike action from the start of the month workers at BHP Billiton’s Spence copper mine in Chile downed tools on the 13<sup>th</sup> after failing to agree to new contract terms with management.  This industrial action is in addition to the ongoing strike at Vale’s Sudbury and Voisey’s Bay operations in Canada (according to Vale’s third quarter report no copper had been produced at either division during Q3 2009).  Added to this, there is the potential for strike action at Codelco’s Andina and Codelco Norte divisions whose contracts expire at the end of November and December respectively.  The Codelco workers will no doubt have raised expectations as a result of the recent Escondida wage settlement. 

**Mine production continues to lag expectation** Prices were also supported by BHP Billiton reporting on the 7<sup>th</sup> that substantial damage had occurred to its main haulage shaft and head frame at it’s Olympic Dam mine in Australia due to mechanical failure.  As a consequence of this damage the company has declared force majeure on some of its copper shipments with mine output restricted to 25% of capacity potentially through to March next year.  We estimate that the loss of production through the remainder of 2009 will be 35kt Cu (See production).  A series of announcements of lowerthan-expected production also provided support for prices.  In Africa, Palabora Mining reported a 15% decline in mined output during Q3 from Q2 while Xstrata, in its Q3 financial results, reported a 9.6% year-on-year decline in mine production.  According to the company, lower output during Q3, which fell from 235kt Cu in Q3 last year to 2

12kt Cu this year, reflected a reduction in ore grade at its Alumbrera, Antamina and Ernest Henry mines. **Concern over the strength of the global recovery persists** Despite the firmer price trend this month market sentiment was dampened, periodically, by concerns over the strength of the global recovery. These concerns were prompted by disappointing economic news, especially in the US where latest data for unemployment, manufacturing activity, factory orders and housing starts were worse than expected. Indeed the news of US home sales in September falling by 3.6% from a month earlier and 7.8% year on year helped lead prices (3m) lower during the latter part of October, down from the month’s high of $6696/t on the 26th to $6465/t at the time of writing. ### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 9000

The price swings that accompanied the changes in open interest suggested alternating periods during which new longs had been established as well as occasions when long positions were liquidated. Overall, while the trend during the past month has been for the establishment of new longs, the interspersed periods of long liquidation suggest that some participants remain somewhat cautious of being too exposed to the upside of this market. ### **Copper LME open interest vs copper price** 270000 7000

**Total exchange stock rise for the fourth consecutive month** Total exchange stocks increased for the fourth consecutive month in October, rising by a net 30.7kt to 523.9kt, as of the 29th . Similar to September, the majority of the gain reflected a net uplift (26.2kt) in LME inventories, to 372.2kt with (unsurprisingly) a large portion of this tonnage (11.2kt) having been delivered into South Korean warehouses. As noted last month, the large build up of tonnage in South Korea is likely to have been material that was originally destined for China. These cathodes have been diverted because of the high level of Chinese imports in recent months and a less favourable arbitrage. Elsewhe

re, LME inventories in European and US locations increased by a net 3.7kt and 7.7kt to 72kt and 232kt respectively.  Meanwhile on Comex, stocks increased by a net 7.2kt (as of the 29<sup>th</sup> ) to 56kt, their highest level since August 2004.  Elsewhere, in China SHFE inventories declined, by a net 2.7kt to ~96kt.  With the exception of last month, exchange stocks held in Shanghai warehouses are at their highest level since April 2004. 

**European spot activity remains slow** There has been no pick up in the European physical spot market with consumers continuing to operate on a hand-to-mouth basis only.  Our sources inform us that there is no fresh demand from any of the end use markets.  Premia are unchanged from last month with Chilean and Grade A material continuing to trade between $70-90/t while standard grade copper commanded a premium of $20-30/t, reflecting ongoing tightness within the high-grade scrap market.  The only small change was in Italy where the price of Livorno warrants declined from $80/t previously to $60/t currently. 

**US and Chinese premia weaken** Similar to Europe, spot activity in the US remains extremely slow as consumers are able to fulfil their anaemic orders from existing long-term contracts.  As a consequence, premia eased during the month from 4-5c/lb delivered Midwest in September to 3.5-4.5c/lb.  Meanwhile in China, premia strengthened during the first half of the month, rising from $55/t in September to $70-80/t.  The improvement reflected a rush for metal following the end of the National Day holiday period which ran from the 1<sup>st</sup> to the 8<sup>th</sup> of October.  However, more recently premia have eased, reflecting rising inventories and slowing demand, and are currently trading between $55-60/t. 

**Codelco concluded term premia in Europe and Asia** In the term market Codelco concluded 2010 contracts with its European customers at a premium of $80/t, the same level as 2009.  The premium set by Codelco, which is an industry benchmark, was well received by other producers who were concerned that the company may have been considering offering a lower rate in light of weakening spot levels.  Meanwhile in Asia, Codelco has agreed 2010 contracts in Japan at $80/t to 85/t, up from $65/t this year.  Finally, Chinese contracts have yet to be concluded but the expectation is that they will be settled around the same level as in Japan.  If achieved, this will represent an increase of 13% from this year’s level of $75/t. 

**Many surprised by Chinese September trade data** One of the biggest surprises of the month was the latest Chinese trade data which showed a 152% uplift in September’s refined copper imports.  A gain of this magnitude had not been

expected given the reduction in SHFE:LME price arbitrage from June onwards and the recent build in SHFE exchange stocks and improved scrap availability.  The la

rge delivery may reflect contracts that were signed earlier in the year, when these were against more favourable arbitrage conditions, but with delivery delayed until September. In addition to the large surge in last month’s net refined copper imports, which totalled 272.1kt, domestic production also increased considerably, up by 18.2% year on year to 375kt, which is a new monthly record. The data suggests that Chinese apparent refined copper consumption had increased by 52% (+220kt) in September from a year earlier. However, at the same time official data showed that Chinese semis production increased by 24.7% year on year in September, implying a significant stock build (regardless of the contribution from scrap). We believe that this mismatch between apparent and real consumption has been a feature of the market throughout the year with cathode inventories in China rising substantially. Our analysis indicates that Chinese cathode stocks will have increased by a forecast ~0.8Mt by year end. In terms of days of global consumption, Chinese refined copper stocks, excluding SHFE inventories, are expected to finish this year at the equivalent of 33 days (see chart below). And while Chinese stocks have doubled from their previous typical levels of 16 days, there has only been a modest uplift in stocks elsewhere (+6 days in exchange warehouses and no change in the world ex-China). This is a really key factor in the sense that the general feel of the market is one of little change in terms of stocks whereas, in reality, both the build up and displacement of inventories into less visible Chinese locations have been massive. ### **Global copper stocks- days of consumption** 80

**Supply will exceed demand by ~1Mt in 2009** Following our LME Week discussions we have revised our global market balance. The revisions reflect steep downward adjustments to a number of our demand estimates. The largest revisions have been made in Europe and the USA (see consumption) where our previously anticipated pick up in demand following the summer shutdown period has not materialised. Our conversations with European producers revealed that the telecom, building wire and autos sectors are all poor with the only real bright area being enamelled wire for white goods. The autos sector is losing momentum with the drawing to a close of the "cash for clunkers" programme. Meanwhile in the US, order books for copper wire rod are reportedly awful given that much of this year's rod consumption has been directed towards the completion of various residential and commercial construction projects that were already underway. Apart from any construction that relates to the government incentive programme there is very little in the way of signific

ant new starts in the private and public sectors. Taking this into account the majority of revisions have occurred in our estimates for Q3 and Q4 as it has become increasingly clear that the previously expected recovery will not occur. Therefore, our global market surpluses have increased to ~140kt and ~220kt in Q3 and Q4 respectively. Previously we were expecting a market deficit of ~-50kt in Q3 and a surplus of ~90kt in Q4. For 2009 as a whole, supply is now forecast to exceed demand by ~0.95Mt, taking stocks to the equivalent of 71 days of consumption by year end (with, as mentioned, 33 days in non-exchange Chinese locations). However, despite the substantial revisions to consumption our 2009 average price forecast of $4964/t ($2.25c/lb) is relatively unchanged from last month given how close we are to the end of this year. **Global surplus forecast** For 2010 we forecast an average price of $5725/t ($2.60c/lb). This is based upon the implicit assumption that there will be only a modest release of speculative stock in China, resulting in a moderate build in inventories elsewhere. As mentioned in previous reports we expect 2010 to be a transitional year with consumption recovering more strongly in 2011 when we expect the market to be in deficit. Prices, reflecting the more favourable outlook, are forecast to rise by 3.9% to average $5950/t ($2.70/lb). Metals Market Service Monthly Update – October 2009 Page 6 of 25 Copper Monthly Update ## Economic Developments **Mixed indicators for global recovery** Economic developments during the month of October continue to paint a mixed picture of the global recovery. Indicators for the Asian economies, notably China and South Korea, go from strength to strength, while in many Western economies the news remains relatively depressed, reinforcing our view that the road to recovery in Europe and the USA will be long and slow. **China GDP growth accelerates** Growth in China’s economy accelerated during the third quarter, with strong investment once again the driving force. GDP growth in the third quarter increased to 8.9% YoY, up from 7.9% in Q2, and taking growth for the first nine months of 2009 to 7.7%. The growth figures highlight the success of, and dependence on, China’s fiscal stimulus package, aimed at offsetting the drop in exports by a surge in spending on fixed assets, and to a lesser extent, consumption. Of the 7.7% growth in China’s GDP in the first three quarters of 2009, investment accounted for 7.3% of growth, and consumption 4%, while the fall in net exports reduced growth by 3.6%. Government funded investment and consumption incentives have also helped industrial production growth continue to gain momentum. IP rose by 13.9% YoY in September, the fastest rate since the summer of 2008. We expect IP growth to continue to accelerate in the coming months, as industrial orders have been steadily rising, and the base effect from slower growth at the end of 2008 kicks in. ### **Chinese fixed asset investment growth (cumulative)** 34%<

**Infrastructure drives fixed asset investment** Fixed asset investment growth in China was very strong in September, and is likely to continue to be strong in the coming months. Many infrastructure projects that had been put on ice during previous years, to prevent an overheating in the economy, are now underway once more. Total fixed asset investment in China has increased by 33.3% year to date, and was up by 35% YoY in September. Investment in transportation has been particularly robust, with investment in railways up 87.5% in the year to September, and in roads by 50.7%. Real estate investment has been much more subdued, however, gaining 17.7% in the first nine months of the year. Encouragingly, investment in health, social security and social welfare has risen by 72.9% YoY in the year to September. Chinese officials have acknowledged the necessity of developing social welfare provisions, which could help to lower China’s precautionary, high domestic savings rate and thus bolster domestic consumption. **South Korean recovery surprises on the upside** South Korea’s economy grew at the fastest pace in seven years during the third quarter. Real Korean GDP expanded by 2.9% from the second quarter and by 0.6% from 3Q08, driven by strong growth in investment, exports and domestic consumption. Machinery and equipment investment increased by 8.9% from Q2, suggesting improved capital spending by firms, although that construction investment is still falling indicates that perhaps large-scale capacity expansions are not yet prevalent. In contrast to China’s heavy fiscal boost, Korean government spending actually decreased through the quarter. The data also showed that Korean output is yet to receive the benefit of restocking. Inventories continued to decrease through the third quarter, albeit at a slower rate than was the case in Q2. **US vehicle sales retract** Auto sales in the USA fell sharply in September following the end to the government’s _Cash for Clunkers_ incentives. Total vehicle sales dropped 40% from August to an annualised rate of 9.2 million units, slightly below the average for the first six months of 2009 of 9.9 million units. The September number was down by 22.7% from a year earlier. Many analysts had been expecting a greater fall in sales, reasoning that the incentive scheme brought forward purchases that would otherwise have taken place in the near future. Meanwhile, US vehicle production rose in Metals Market Service Monthly Update – October 2009 Page 7 of 25 Copper Monthly Update September to 654k units, its highest level since October 2008, and gained 17% from August and 126% from the nadir reached in January. The boost to sales provided by the _Cash f

or Clunkers_ scheme further depleted already low inventory levels at showrooms across the USA, resulting in the need for higher vehicle production to rebuild inventories to more manageable levels. However, now that the scheme has drawn to a close and sales have declined, it is questionable whether vehicle output can continue to recover through the end of the year. ### **USA monthly vehicle production and sales** 1800

**Currency appreciation weighs on European recovery** The major euro zone economies have started to recover and we expect that GDP data released in the coming month will show that the euro zone emerged from recession during the third quarter. The recovery in Germany, amongst others, has been driven by improving exports, and many expect improving exports to be the lead driver in the euro zone recovery through into 2010. However, having risen steadily through the second quarter, Germany’s exports and trade surplus both declined in August. The goods trade balance was €10.6bn in August, compared with €12.5bn in July. One of the key drags on improving exports in Europe is the continued appreciation of the euro, which has strengthened by over 16% in nominal terms against the US$ since March, reducing the competitiveness of European exports. We anticipate the euro will continue appreciating against the dollar in the near term, threatening the manufacturing recovery that has begun to emerge. ### **Euro per US dollar** 0.85

Metals Market Service Monthly Update – October 2009 Page 8 of 25 Copper Monthly Update ## Consumption **Manufacturing indices strengthen in September** The global economy continues to emerge from recession, highlighted by strong manufacturing indices for September and an upward revision in the IMF’s world growth forecast for next year. During September the Institute of Supply Management (ISM) reported that its headline index in the US remained above 50, the level that separates expansion from contraction, for the second consecutive month. Likewise in China, the Purchasing Managers index (PMI) rose for the fourth consecutive month, up from 54 in August to 54.3. Also encouraging was the Chinese output component of the index which reached a new high for the year, up from 57.9 in August to 58. Meanwhile in Europe, the PMI remained below the all important expansion level of 50. However, the reading of 49.3 was up sharply from 48.2 in August and represented a 16-month high. In tandem with the positive results the IMF recently increased its forecast for

global economic growth for this year, lifting it from its July forecast of 2.5% to 3.1%. According to the IMF the upward revision followed stimulus packages in excess of $2tr. **Copper demand remains weak in some regions** Despite the improving global economic picture, demand for copper in some regions remains extremely weak. This is especially true of Europe and the USA where the downturn in some markets has been much stronger than we previously anticipated. As a consequence we have lowered our Western European and US forecasts for this year by a net 240kt and 202kt respectively. In contrast we have raised our forecasts for China and the CIS, reflecting stronger demand than previously expected, by ~260kt and ~75kt respectively. Thus we now estimate that global demand for copper will decrease by 4.5% this year, to ~17.1Mt, before recovering by 4.4% in 2010 and 6.3 % in 2011 to ~17.9Mt and ~19Mt respectively. As noted previously, the stronger recovery in 2011 reflects growing demand from the construction sector. While construction activity is expected to recover in 2010, the positive impact that this will have on copper demand will not be fully realised until the following year. This is because copper wire and cable and copper plumbing and heating tube are not installed in any new build until the latter stages of construction. **European demand for copper disappoints** According to our sources, European demand for copper has weakened following the summer shutdown period. This partly reflected falling orders from the auto sector. Prior to the shutdown period orders for automotive wire were reported to have improved from May through to August. However, this upward momentum was not maintained in September with orders falling off sharply. This reflected falling car sales in light of some government car scrappage schemes coming to an end. As a consequence one wire producer reported that his production of automotive wire is expected to fall by 15% this year. ### **Production and shipments of copper wire rod and copper semis – (kt)** ||**2007**|**2008**|**2008**

**Double digit decline forecast in European wire rod production** In tandem with falling demand for drawn copper wire, Western European production of copper wire rod is also expected to decline by 14-15% this year.  Although some producers will fare better than others, depending upon which markets they supply.  For example, one major wire rod producer that we spoke to is expecting production this year to be equal to last year.  This is due to him supplying the high tension power cable market which has not been so badly affected by the global crisis.  However, other producers are not so fortunate, as highlighted by Nexan’s recent decision to close its 300kt/a Chauny wire rod plant in France at the beginning of next year because of falling demand and over capacity.  Indeed latest reports suggest that the Chauny wire rod plant is currently running at only 150kt/a because of the strike action which broke out following the company’s announcement of the forthcoming closure. 

**Wire rod negotiations very subdued during LME week** In light of the poor market conditions, wire rod producers reported that contract negotiations for next year were subdued during LME week with many of their customers uncertain about their requirements for next year.  As a consequence orders for next year were very conservative with many (customers) preferring to operate on a hand-to-mouth due to no immediate recovery in demand. 

**Rising credit insurance costs may be an issue for European wire rod market next year** Another factor likely to plague the wire rod market next year is rising credit insurance costs.  One wire rod producer explained that during the first two months of next year credit insurance for some wire rod producers is due to expire and they are unlikely to renew it because it is too expensive.  Credit insurance has risen in tandem with rising copper prices and, according to our sources, can add 5 euros/t to the overall price of the copper wire rod.  Nevertheless, in today’s uncertain market it is very difficult to trade without this.  Therefore, if producers do not have it then they will be pushing for much reduced payment terms or even cash in advance.  However, consumers will be looking for extended payment terms meaning that those producers without credit insurance could lose out on market share.  Thus next year could be a very difficult year for some wire rod producers with further closures a possibility.

**Chinese concentrate imports on track for 6.3Mdmt in 2009** Copper concentrates have continued to enter Chinese ports at near record rates.  September’s receipts of 562kdmt were the second highest on record bringing the cumulative nine-month total to 4.69Mdmt (+19.8% year on year).  This is directly in line with our forecast overall growth (+20%) in 2009 Chinese copper concentrate imports of 6.3Mdmt.  The most significant gains in tonnage terms thus far in 2009 have been seen from Kazakhstan (+159kt), Australia (+127kt), Laos (+127kt), Iran (+99kt) and Canada (+98kt).  There are now three key Kazakh suppliers; Kazzinc (Zyrianovsk and Ridder), Russian Copper Company (Koktaus) and Kazakhmys (Zhezkazgan).  The latter is now a supplier to the custom concentrate market after the company decided that it would be cheaper to sell concentrates than to run the both electric furnaces in the Zhezkazgan smelter at suboptimal rates. 

**Quiet start to the annual Mating Season** As usual, LME Week marked the official opening of the annual copper concentrate Mating Season.  These negotiations have been particularly tough for buyers because of the wide acceptance amongst market participants of the profound overcapacity that now exists within the primary smelting sector. It seems that the initial discussions have focussed less upon the outlook for the market and more on what level of TC/RCs smelters require in order to be viable, particularly in light of the exceedingly poor medium-term prospects for the sulphuric acid market.  From our discussions with buyers and sellers it would appear that as yet no numbers have been officially tabled.  Ideally, smelters would like a rollover of last year’s settlements ($75/t & 7.5c/lb) or, at worst terms in the mid 60s & 6s.  We would suspect that miners will be seeking to conclude deals at somewhat below the recent mid-year

market rate of $50/t & 5c/lb.  No doubt there will be a little more clarity on Mating Season developments following BHP Billiton’s next round of meetings in Tokyo in the middle of next month. 

**Acid and scrap have become increasingly important to primary smelters** The impact of acid prices on primary copper smelting economics has become far more critical over time.  This is because, while the average copper content of internationally traded concentrates has declined from a peak of 30.5% in 2000, to 26.5% currently, the average sulphur content has been increasing.  As an example, the average copper:sulphur ratio for the five major Japanese custom smelters has declined from 1.14:1 in 2000, to 1.05:1 in 2004 and to 0.92:1 in 2008.  Assuming 100% sulphur capture and an average copper smelter recovery of 98.5% this means that for every tonne of primary copper produced in Japan the equivalent output of acid has increased from 2.73t in 2000, to 2.97t in 2004 and to 3.37t in 2008.  The change over time in copper:sulphur ratio also has an impact on primary smelter heat balances with more sulphur needing to be burnt off at the converting stage and thereby raising converter temperatures.  And, with less copper being returned to the converters in the form of refinery scrap anodes (due to the fall in copper content of concentrates), smelters have raised the amount of purchased scrap to assist with the cooling process.  The contribution of copper from purchased scrap to overall new anode output at concentrate consuming smelters has risen from 9.5% in 2000 to almost 13.5% in 2008.  In this manner, purchased scrap is melted “for free” and hence the cost of producing anodes from these secondary sources is limited to materials handling and casting.  The profit from these secondary feed sources has been a particularly useful offset to low TC/RCs in recent years.  However, the economics of scrap processing is heavily dependent upon the differential between the scrap price and LME/Comex metal quotes with this “spread” widening and contracting in response to scrap supply/demand dynamics. 

**Chinese gears up for massive increase in secondary smelting and refining capacity** As alluded to last month China’s plans to expand its secondary smelting and refining industry are somewhat alarming in the context of the overall size of these markets which has potentially profound implications for scrap spreads moving forward.  This year we estimate that global consumption of smelter and refinery grade scrap will decline by 16% relative to 2008 (i.e. from 3.2Mt to 2.7Mt) due to lack of supply during the first half of this year.  On the basis of recently announced Chinese brownfield and greenfield secondary smelter/refinery developments (see table below) the country is set to add 1.7Mt/a of processing capacity within the next five years, which is equivalent to almost two thirds of current scrap supplies.  Under these circumstances the outlook for the secondary smelting and refi

ning industries looks poised to mirror what has happened in primary smelting, i.e. trending towards an untenable overall level of processing capacity.  This is likely to reduce scrap spreads dramatically and will also result in a significant increase in market volatility with Chinese scrap buying patterns heavily influenced by the (highly variable) arbitrage between SHFE prices and international quotes.

## Production news 

**Spence mine on strike – no resolution at Vale Inco either** Some 560 unionised workers at the 200kt/a Spence mine in Chile went on strike on October 13<sup>th</sup> after rejecting BHP Billiton’s pay offer.  Mining and agglomerating activities were halted immediately although leaching and production have been maintained at levels that ensure process and asset integrity.  Meanwhile the strikes at Vale Inco’s Sudbury and Voisey’s Bay operations are ongoing with neither site contributing to Vale’s copper output during Q3 2009.  For the first nine months of this year Sudbury’s copper production fell by 48kt year on year while for Voisey’s Bay the figure was 15kt lower.  That said the company will report some output in Q4 having resumed partial operations at the Clarabelle mill fed by high grade copper ores from the Coleman and Garson mines as well as material from FNX Mining’s operations.  Elsewhere Inmet Mining has forthcoming labour negotiations at its 30kt/a Cayeli mine and its new 72kt/a Las Cruces SxEw operation. 

**Main shaft out of action at Olympic Dam** BHP Billiton has declared force majeure on domestic cathode shipments from its Olympic Dam complex following the breakdown of the main underground haulage system on October 6<sup>th</sup> .  The incident occurred in the Clark shaft, which accounts for 80% of the mine’s ore haulage.  It seems that the automated skip breaking system failed causing a skip to plummet at high speed into the bottom of the shaft and resulted in a counterweight being propelled into the main head gear.  The extent of the damage is still being assessed and initial indications are that repairs will take three to six months.  In the meantime, ore haulage is being carried out in the smaller Whenan shaft but at 20-25% of the mine’s normal capacity.  The smelter/refinery will have to be operated on a campaign basis and the company may advance a maintenance shutdown into Q1 2010.  Lost output is currently estimated to be 35kt Cu over the remainder of 2009.  In 2008 the complex produced 191.4kt of copper cathodes.

f production.  Probable reserves have been put at 661Mt grading 0.50% Cu, 0.12g/t Au, 0.013% Mo and 2.51g/t Ag.  Minmetals owns 60% of the project with the balance being held by Jiangxi Copper.  The joint venture partners expect to spend $1-1.5Bn developing the 90kt/d open pit mine and conventional mill project.  A framework financing deal was signed in November 2008 with China Development Bank and Banco de Credito.

Elsewhere Sumitomo Metal Mining expects production to remain fairly constant at 201kt (200kt) while Mitsubishi Materials forecasts a 7.3% rise to 156.1kt (145.6kt) following completion to repairs to its 51%-owned Onahama smelter.  Meanwhile Dowa Mining will raise output by 6.9% to 55.9kt (40.2kt), Furukawa Mining by +6.7% to 43.4kt (40.6ktt) and Nittetsu by +10.2% to 21.7kt (19.7kt).  According to our estimates overall Japanese refined production is forecast to decline by almost 5% (year on year) in 2009, from 1.54Mt Cu to 1.465Mt Cu. 

**Codelco raises 9M 2009 output by 15%** Codelco, the world’s largest copper producer has seen a 15% year-on-year increase in its nine month copper production, from 1.107Mt to 1.274Mt Cu.  At the Nortй division production was 613kt in the Jan-Sept 2009 period (compared with 552kt a year earlier).  Elsewhere, output at Salvador was 46kt (36kt), Andina 159kt (159kt), El Teniente 286kt (271kt) and Gaby 110kt (36kt).  Codelco’s 49% share of El Abra production added a further 59kt (61kt).  Note that these production figures relate to commercial production (cathodes, blister/anodes and copper-in-concentrates) and hence they are a hybrid of metal contained and recoverable copper.
